cards.front: What should you know about respiration?
cards.back: An exothermic reaction in which glucose is broken down to release energy for living processes. Respiration happens in every living cell, all the time.

cards.front: What should you know about aerobic respiration?
cards.back: uses oxygen to break down glucose completely. It releases a large amount of energy and takes place in the mitochondria.

cards.front: What should you know about key points?
cards.back: Aerobic respiration releases much more energy per glucose molecule than anaerobic respiration It happens in the mitochondria (cells with high energy needs have many mitochondria, e.g. muscle cells, sperm cells) It is an exothermic reaction (releases energy to the surroundings) Energy released is used for: muscle contraction, protein synthesis, cell division, active transport, maintaining body temperature

cards.front: What should you know about anaerobic respiration?
cards.back: takes place without oxygen. In animal cells (including human muscle cells), glucose is broken down into lactic acid. It releases much less energy than aerobic respiration because the glucose is only partially broken down.

cards.front: What should you know about when does anaerobic respiration happen??
cards.back: During vigorous exercise, the body cannot supply enough oxygen to the muscles for aerobic respiration alone. The muscles switch to anaerobic respiration to provide extra energy, producing lactic acid.

cards.front: What should you know about fermentation?
cards.back: is anaerobic respiration in yeast and some microorganisms. Glucose is broken down into ethanol and carbon dioxide. This process is used in brewing and baking.

cards.front: What should you know about applications of fermentation?
cards.back: Brewing: Yeast ferments sugar in barley to produce ethanol (alcohol) and CO₂ Baking: Yeast ferments sugar in dough. The CO₂ produced makes the bread rise. The ethanol evaporates during baking.

cards.front: What should you know about oxygen debt?
cards.back: The extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down the lactic acid that has built up in the muscles. The lactic acid is transported to the liver, where it is converted back to glucose using oxygen.

cards.front: What should you know about how oxygen debt is repaid?
cards.back: After exercise, breathing rate and heart rate remain high to deliver extra oxygen to the liver The liver uses this oxygen to convert lactic acid back to glucose Blood flow through the muscles is also increased to transport lactic acid to the liver This is why you continue to breathe heavily after stopping exercise

cards.front: What should you know about metabolism?
cards.back: The sum of all the chemical reactions in a cell or in the body. Metabolic reactions include both breakdown (catabolic) and building (anabolic) reactions. Many metabolic reactions are controlled by enzymes.

cards.front: What should you know about examples of metabolic reactions?
cards.back: Conversion of glucose to starch, glycogen or cellulose Formation of lipids from glycerol and fatty acids Formation of amino acids from glucose and nitrates (in plants) Respiration Photosynthesis Breakdown of excess proteins to form urea (in the liver)
